questions.title: How many ATP does one glucose molecule yield under full aerobic oxidation, versus anaerobic glycolysis alone, and how much of the aerobic total is made at the substrate level within glycolysis itself?
questions.question: How many ATP does one glucose molecule yield under full aerobic oxidation, versus anaerobic glycolysis alone, and how much of the aerobic total is made at the substrate level within glycolysis itself?

options.A: 32 ATP aerobically, 2 ATP anaerobically; 4 of the aerobic ATP are made at the substrate level within glycolysis
options.B: 38 ATP aerobically, 8 ATP anaerobically; none of it is made at the substrate level
options.C: 32 ATP aerobically, 0 ATP anaerobically; all of it is made at the substrate level
options.D: 2 ATP aerobically, 32 ATP anaerobically; 4 are made at the substrate level

explanations.A: Correct. Complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule, via glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, yields about 32 ATP using the modern shuttle-corrected accounting; anaerobic glycolysis alone, without the mitochondria to reoxidise NADH, nets only 2 ATP. Within glycolysis itself, four ATP are generated by substrate-level phosphorylation (two per triose, at the phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase steps), though two of those four are spent paying back the pathway's own priming steps, leaving glycolysis's own net contribution at 2 ATP either way.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The commonly quoted older figure of 38 ATP overcounts the cost of shuttling cytosolic NADH into the mitochondrion; the modern, shuttle-corrected total is about 32. Some ATP genuinely is made at the substrate level (four within glycolysis, one more in the citric acid cycle), so 'none' is also wrong.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Anaerobic glycolysis does yield ATP (2 net), just far less than the aerobic total; and while substrate-level phosphorylation contributes ATP, most of the aerobic total actually comes from oxidative phosphorylation at the electron transport chain, not from substrate-level reactions alone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This reverses the aerobic and anaerobic totals; aerobic oxidation yields far more ATP than anaerobic glycolysis, not less.

questions.learning_objective: State the aerobic (32) versus anaerobic (2) ATP yield per glucose and that four glycolytic ATP are made at the substrate level.
questions.source_citation: EOM - Blood end wafdeen final, Q19-20 (Alexandria University, AU-MED-103); EOM - Blood Final Egyptian final, Q1.

questions.title: Why does anaerobic glycolysis convert pyruvate to lactate, when lactate itself has no further metabolic use in that cell?
questions.question: Why does anaerobic glycolysis convert pyruvate to lactate, when lactate itself has no further metabolic use in that cell?

options.A: To regenerate the NAD+ that glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase needs, since anaerobic conditions leave no mitochondrial route to reoxidise NADH
options.B: To generate one additional ATP directly from the reaction
options.C: To detoxify pyruvate, which is otherwise harmful to the cell
options.D: To provide the substrate for gluconeogenesis in the same cell

explanations.A: Correct. Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, one of glycolysis's own steps, consumes NAD+ and produces NADH; without oxygen and functioning mitochondria to reoxidise that NADH back to NAD+ via the electron transport chain, the cell's small NAD+ pool would be exhausted within seconds and glycolysis would grind to a halt. Converting pyruvate to lactate via lactate dehydrogenase regenerates NAD+ directly in the cytosol, at the cost of no extra energy, purely so glycolysis itself can keep running — the lactate produced is not being made for its own sake, it is a by-product of solving this redox problem.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lactate dehydrogenase reaction produces no ATP of its own; its only purpose is regenerating NAD+, not adding to the pathway's energy yield.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pyruvate is not toxic to the cell; the reaction exists to solve a redox (NAD+ supply) problem, not a detoxification one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lactate produced this way is typically exported for use elsewhere (such as the Cori cycle, where the liver converts it back to glucose); it is not retained by the same cell as a gluconeogenic substrate.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that anaerobic glycolysis makes lactate to regenerate NAD+ for glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, not for lactate's own sake.
questions.source_citation: EOM - Blood End Egyptian 1, Q14 (Alexandria University, AU-MED-103).

questions.title: The citric acid cycle is described as a "cycle" even though several of its individual reactions are irreversible. What actually makes it cyclic?
questions.question: The citric acid cycle is described as a "cycle" even though several of its individual reactions are irreversible. What actually makes it cyclic?

options.A: Every one of its reactions is freely reversible in both directions
options.B: Oxaloacetate is regenerated at the end of every turn, ready to condense with a fresh acetyl-CoA
options.C: The cycle only runs cyclically under anaerobic conditions
options.D: Citrate is regenerated at the end of every turn instead of oxaloacetate

explanations.A: Incorrect. Several citric acid cycle reactions (citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) are strongly irreversible under cellular conditions; the cycle's circularity does not depend on every step running backwards.
explanations.B: Correct. What makes the pathway a cycle is that oxaloacetate, condensed away at the very first step to form citrate, is regenerated by the end of each full turn (via succinate to fumarate to malate to oxaloacetate) and is then ready to accept another acetyl-CoA and start the next turn. The cycle's irreversible steps drive it forward in one direction each turn; it is oxaloacetate's continuous regeneration, not step-by-step reversibility, that closes the loop.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The citric acid cycle is an obligately aerobic pathway (it depends on the electron transport chain to reoxidise the NADH and FADH2 it produces); it does not run under anaerobic conditions at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Citrate is the product of the first step, consumed as the cycle proceeds; it is oxaloacetate, not citrate, that is regenerated at the end of each turn.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that the citric acid cycle is cyclic because oxaloacetate regenerates every turn, not because its individual reactions are reversible.
questions.source_citation: Background fact underlying the already-tested CAC-ATP-yield and amphibolic-role questions (Alexandria University, AU-MED-103); MCQs - CHO Metabolism MCQs (1), general CAC cluster.

questions.title: A well-fed liver cell has abundant fatty acids available for oxidation. How does this state affect the balance between glycolysis and gluconeogenesis in that cell?
questions.question: A well-fed liver cell has abundant fatty acids available for oxidation. How does this state affect the balance between glycolysis and gluconeogenesis in that cell?

options.A: It has no effect; glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are regulated entirely independently of fatty acid oxidation
options.B: Fatty acid oxidation raises acetyl-CoA and ATP, which inhibit glycolysis's regulatory enzymes and activate gluconeogenesis's, tipping the balance towards making glucose
options.C: Fatty acid oxidation always tips the balance towards glycolysis, regardless of energy state
options.D: Fatty acid oxidation is only relevant to muscle, never to liver glucose metabolism

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fatty acid oxidation is a major input into the reciprocal glycolysis/gluconeogenesis switch in liver, not an unrelated process.
explanations.B: Correct. When the liver is oxidising fatty acids briskly (as it does during fasting, or when supplied with a high fat load), the resulting rise in acetyl-CoA and ATP inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase and PFK-1 (glycolysis's key enzymes) while activating pyruvate carboxylase (a gluconeogenic enzyme, allosterically switched on by acetyl-CoA). The net effect is that active fatty acid oxidation tips the liver's own glucose metabolism towards making glucose rather than breaking it down — physiologically sensible, since a fasting liver oxidising fat for its own energy needs should be exporting glucose to the rest of the body, not consuming it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is the opposite of the actual regulation; fatty acid oxidation tips the balance towards gluconeogenesis, not glycolysis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This reciprocal relationship is specifically a liver phenomenon central to whole-body glucose homeostasis during fasting, not a muscle-only effect.

questions.learning_objective: Explain how fatty acid oxidation (via acetyl-CoA and ATP) reciprocally inhibits glycolysis and activates gluconeogenesis in the liver.
questions.source_citation: EOM - Blood End Egyptian 1, Q19 (Alexandria University, AU-MED-103); EOM - Blood Final Egyptian final, Q11.

questions.title: Which two tissues does the body's glucose supply exist mainly to protect, and why does this drive the need for gluconeogenesis?
questions.question: Which two tissues does the body's glucose supply exist mainly to protect, and why does this drive the need for gluconeogenesis?

options.A: Red blood cells and the brain, since red cells have no mitochondria and depend on glucose absolutely, and the brain relies very heavily on it too
options.B: Skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, since both depend on glucose absolutely and cannot use any other fuel
options.C: The liver and kidney, since both organs cannot survive without a constant external glucose supply
options.D: The skin and bone marrow, since both organs are the most glucose-dependent tissues in the body

explanations.A: Correct. Red blood cells, lacking mitochondria entirely, can only make ATP by glycolysis and are therefore absolutely dependent on a continuous glucose supply with no alternative fuel option; the brain, while it can adapt to ketone bodies during prolonged starvation, relies very heavily on glucose under normal conditions and cannot tolerate a sudden drop. Gluconeogenesis exists largely to keep blood glucose from falling below the level these two tissues need, during the hours between meals and especially during fasting or starvation, when dietary glucose is unavailable.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Skeletal muscle and adipose tissue can both use fatty acids as an alternative fuel and are not absolutely glucose-dependent the way red cells are.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The liver is in fact the organ that performs gluconeogenesis to supply glucose to other tissues, not a tissue that depends on an external glucose supply itself; the kidney also contributes some gluconeogenesis rather than depending entirely on outside glucose.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Skin and bone marrow are not singled out as the tissues gluconeogenesis exists to protect; the defining absolutely-glucose-dependent tissue is the red blood cell, with the brain as the other major glucose-reliant tissue.

questions.learning_objective: Name red blood cells and the brain as the tissues gluconeogenesis exists mainly to protect, and explain why red cells are absolutely glucose-dependent.

questions.title: Substrate-level phosphorylation makes ATP directly, without the electron transport chain. At which three reactions does this happen in central carbohydrate metabolism?
questions.question: Substrate-level phosphorylation makes ATP directly, without the electron transport chain. At which three reactions does this happen in central carbohydrate metabolism?

options.A: Phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase in glycolysis, and succinate thiokinase (succinyl-CoA synthetase) in the citric acid cycle
options.B: Hexokinase and phosphofructokinase-1 in glycolysis, and citrate synthase in the citric acid cycle
options.C: All ten glycolytic reactions and all eight citric acid cycle reactions equally
options.D: Only the electron transport chain's ATP synthase step

explanations.A: Correct. Substrate-level phosphorylation directly transfers a high-energy phosphate from a reaction intermediate to ADP, without any involvement of the electron transport chain or a proton gradient. In glycolysis this happens twice per glucose, once at phosphoglycerate kinase (1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate) and once at pyruvate kinase (phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate); in the citric acid cycle it happens once, at succinate thiokinase (succinyl-CoA synthetase), which actually produces GTP rather than ATP directly (interconvertible with ATP via nucleoside diphosphate kinase).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hexokinase and PFK-1 consume ATP rather than produce it, and citrate synthase produces no high-energy phosphate at all; none of these three is a substrate-level phosphorylation site.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Most glycolytic and citric acid cycle reactions do not generate ATP or GTP directly; only the three specific reactions named above do.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ATP synthase's action is oxidative phosphorylation, driven by the proton gradient the electron transport chain builds -- the opposite of substrate-level phosphorylation, which makes ATP without that gradient.

questions.learning_objective: Name the three substrate-level phosphorylation reactions of central carbohydrate metabolism: phosphoglycerate kinase, pyruvate kinase, and succinate thiokinase.

questions.title: The hexose monophosphate shunt has two phases. What does its non-oxidative phase produce, and why does the cell need this product?
questions.question: The hexose monophosphate shunt has two phases. What does its non-oxidative phase produce, and why does the cell need this product?

options.A: Ribose-5-phosphate, needed for nucleotide and nucleic acid synthesis
options.B: NADPH, needed for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defence
options.C: ATP, needed to drive the oxidative phase forward
options.D: Glucose-6-phosphate, regenerated to restart the shunt

explanations.A: Correct. The hexose monophosphate shunt's oxidative phase (glucose-6-phosphate through 6-phosphogluconate to ribulose-5-phosphate) generates NADPH and is irreversible; its separate non-oxidative phase then rearranges the resulting pentose sugars, via transketolase and transaldolase reactions, to yield ribose-5-phosphate, the sugar every cell needs to build the ribose backbone of nucleotides, RNA and DNA. A cell that needs mainly NADPH (for fat synthesis, for example) can run the oxidative phase alone and let the non-oxidative phase's reactions run in reverse to recycle any excess pentose back to glycolytic intermediates; a rapidly dividing cell that needs mainly ribose-5-phosphate can favour the non-oxidative route instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. NADPH is the product of the shunt's oxidative phase, not its non-oxidative phase; the two phases have genuinely different outputs.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The hexose monophosphate shunt produces no ATP at any point, in either phase.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glucose-6-phosphate is the shunt's starting substrate, consumed at the very first step of the oxidative phase, not a product regenerated by the non-oxidative phase.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the HMP shunt's oxidative phase (NADPH) from its non-oxidative phase (ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis).
questions.source_citation: MCQs - CHO Metabolism MCQs (1), Q84-85, Q41-42, Q88 (Alexandria University, AU-MED-103).

questions.title: HbA1c formation is non-enzymatic glycation. At which specific site on the haemoglobin molecule does glucose attach to form HbA1c?
questions.question: HbA1c formation is non-enzymatic glycation. At which specific site on the haemoglobin molecule does glucose attach to form HbA1c?

options.A: The N-terminal valine of the beta chain
options.B: The C-terminal histidine of the alpha chain
options.D: A random internal lysine residue with no consistent site

explanations.A: Correct. HbA1c forms when glucose attaches non-enzymatically to the N-terminal valine of the beta globin chain, first forming a reversible Schiff base and then rearranging into a stable ketoamine linkage. Because this reaction is slow, irreversible once rearranged, and proportional to the average glucose concentration the red cell has been exposed to over its roughly 120-day lifespan, the resulting HbA1c fraction is a reliable index of average glycaemic control over the preceding two to three months.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The reaction occurs at the beta chain's N-terminal valine, not at the alpha chain's C-terminus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glycation attaches glucose to the globin protein itself, not to the haem iron, which remains unaffected by this modification.
explanations.D: Incorrect. HbA1c formation is not random; it occurs specifically and consistently at the beta chain's N-terminal valine, which is exactly what makes it a reproducible, standardised clinical marker rather than an unpredictable one.

questions.learning_objective: State the N-terminal valine of the beta chain as the specific glycation site that forms HbA1c.
questions.source_citation: MCQs - Blood Agha MCQ, Q40 (Alexandria University, AU-MED-103).

questions.title: Epinephrine and glucagon both raise blood glucose by acting on liver glycogen. What is the shared covalent mechanism by which they do this?
questions.question: Epinephrine and glucagon both raise blood glucose by acting on liver glycogen. What is the shared covalent mechanism by which they do this?

options.A: A cAMP-driven protein kinase A cascade that phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase, while phosphorylating and inactivating glycogen synthase at the same time
options.B: Direct allosteric binding of the hormone itself to glycogen phosphorylase, with no signalling cascade involved
options.C: Dephosphorylation of glycogen phosphorylase, which activates it
options.D: A cascade that activates both glycogen phosphorylase and glycogen synthase simultaneously

explanations.A: Correct. Both epinephrine and glucagon bind their own receptors and raise intracellular cAMP, which activates protein kinase A; protein kinase A then phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase (switching it ON, since phosphorylase is active in its phosphorylated form) and, in the same cascade, phosphorylates glycogen synthase (switching it OFF, since synthase is active in its dephosphorylated form). This single covalent-modification cascade therefore simultaneously promotes glycogen breakdown and shuts down glycogen synthesis, exactly the coordinated response needed to raise blood glucose quickly.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neither hormone binds glycogen phosphorylase directly; both act through a cell-surface receptor and a cAMP/protein kinase A signalling cascade.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This reverses the actual covalent change; glycogen phosphorylase is activated by phosphorylation, not dephosphorylation, under this cascade.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cascade activates phosphorylase while simultaneously inactivating synthase, not activating both together, which is exactly what makes the response coordinated rather than self-defeating.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the shared cAMP/protein kinase A cascade by which epinephrine and glucagon activate phosphorylase and inactivate synthase together.
questions.source_citation: MCQs - CHO Metabolism MCQs (1), Q108, Q78, Q93, Q97 (Alexandria University, AU-MED-103).

questions.title: A red cell inherits a deficiency of pyruvate kinase. What is the biochemical consequence, and what disease does it cause?
questions.question: A red cell inherits a deficiency of pyruvate kinase. What is the biochemical consequence, and what disease does it cause?

options.A: The red cell makes no net ATP from glucose, causing a hereditary haemolytic anaemia
options.B: The red cell makes double its normal ATP yield, causing polycythaemia
options.C: The red cell can no longer bind oxygen, causing methaemoglobinaemia
options.D: The red cell loses its ability to make 2,3-BPG, with no effect on ATP yield

explanations.A: Correct. Pyruvate kinase catalyses the last, and one of only two, substrate-level phosphorylation steps of glycolysis; without it, the red cell -- which depends on glycolysis as its only ATP source, having no mitochondria -- makes no net ATP from glucose at all. The resulting energy failure shortens red cell survival and causes a chronic hereditary haemolytic anaemia, the second most common enzyme-deficiency cause of hereditary haemolytic anaemia after G6PD deficiency, but arising by a completely different mechanism (energy failure rather than oxidant vulnerability).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Losing a step that makes ATP reduces, rather than doubles, the pathway's net ATP yield, and the clinical consequence is anaemia (fewer functional red cells), not polycythaemia (excess red cells).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pyruvate kinase deficiency is an energy-metabolism defect, not a hameoglobin oxidation-state defect; oxygen binding itself is unaffected, distinguishing it from methaemoglobinaemia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 2,3-BPG synthesis branches off earlier in glycolysis, upstream of the pyruvate kinase step, so it is not directly abolished by this deficiency; and the deficiency's defining consequence is exactly the loss of net ATP yield, not something separate from it.

questions.learning_objective: Explain why pyruvate kinase deficiency abolishes net glycolytic ATP yield in the red cell, causing hereditary haemolytic anaemia.

questions.title: Which enzyme is described as the rate-limiting step of glycogen degradation (glycogenolysis)?
questions.question: Which enzyme is described as the rate-limiting step of glycogen degradation (glycogenolysis)?

explanations.A: Correct. Glycogen phosphorylase, which removes glucose units one at a time from glycogen's outer branches as glucose-1-phosphate, is the rate-limiting and most tightly regulated enzyme of glycogenolysis, controlled by the same cAMP/covalent-phosphorylation cascade that reciprocally shuts down glycogen synthase. Debranching enzyme plays a necessary but secondary role, clearing the last few residues at each branch point so phosphorylase can continue, but it is phosphorylase's own activity that sets the pathway's overall pace.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Debranching enzyme is essential for complete breakdown at branch points, but it is not the pathway's rate-limiting, regulated step; that role belongs to glycogen phosphorylase.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glycogen synthase is the key regulated enzyme of glycogen synthesis (the opposite pathway), not of glycogen degradation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hexokinase acts on free glucose entering glycolysis; it plays no role in breaking down glycogen itself.

questions.learning_objective: Identify glycogen phosphorylase as the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenolysis, distinct from debranching enzyme's supporting role.
questions.source_citation: EOM - Blood End Egyptian 1, Q8 (Alexandria University, AU-MED-103); EOM - Blood Final Egyptian final, Q14-15.

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT a genuine intermediate of the citric acid cycle?
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a genuine intermediate of the citric acid cycle?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a genuine intermediate). Alpha-ketoglutarate is formed from isocitrate and is itself decarboxylated to succinyl-CoA, a core step of the cycle.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a genuine intermediate). Succinate is produced from succinyl-CoA at the cycle's one substrate-level phosphorylation step and is then oxidised to fumarate.
explanations.C: Correct -- acetoacetate is NOT a citric acid cycle intermediate. Acetoacetate is a ketone body, made from acetyl-CoA in the liver during fasting or ketosis, and it belongs to fatty-acid-derived ketone body metabolism, an entirely separate pathway from the eight-step ring of citrate, isocitrate, alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, succinate, fumarate, malate and oxaloacetate. A question that lists three genuine cycle members alongside one plausible-sounding acetyl-CoA-derived molecule is testing exactly this: knowing the cycle's own eight-member list precisely enough to spot the outsider.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS a genuine intermediate). Malate is formed from fumarate and is oxidised to regenerate oxaloacetate, completing the cycle.

questions.learning_objective: Identify acetoacetate (a ketone body) as not a genuine citric acid cycle intermediate, distinguishing the cycle's own eight members from a metabolically adjacent molecule.
questions.source_citation: MCQs - CHO Metabolism MCQs (1), Q53-54 (Alexandria University, AU-MED-103).

questions.title: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) contains which metal at the centre of its corrin ring, and which two human enzymes require it as coenzyme?
questions.question: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) contains which metal at the centre of its corrin ring, and which two human enzymes require it as coenzyme?

options.A: Cobalt; methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase
options.B: Iron; methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase
options.C: Cobalt; dihydrofolate reductase and thymidylate synthase

explanations.A: Correct. Vitamin B12 is named for the cobalt atom held at the centre of its corrin ring, the feature that distinguishes it structurally from haem's iron-centred porphyrin ring. In humans, only two enzymes require a B12-derived coenzyme: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (using adenosylcobalamin, converting methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in fatty acid and amino acid catabolism) and methionine synthase (using methylcobalamin, remethylating homocysteine to methionine). This is why B12 deficiency has two distinct biochemical consequences: raised methylmalonic acid from the first enzyme's failure, and raised homocysteine plus impaired one-carbon/DNA synthesis from the second's.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The metal at cobalamin's core is cobalt, not iron; iron is haem's defining metal, a different molecule entirely.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dihydrofolate reductase and thymidylate synthase are folate-pathway enzymes, not B12-dependent ones; B12's two human enzymes are methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cobalamin's metal is cobalt, not zinc, and B12 has two dependent human enzymes, not one.

questions.learning_objective: State that cobalt is B12's central metal and name methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase as its two human coenzyme-dependent enzymes.
questions.source_citation: MCQs - Blood Agha MCQ, Q20, Q44, Q72 (Alexandria University, AU-MED-103); EOM - Blood End Egyptian 1, Q9.

questions.title: Why are strict vegetarians at particular risk of vitamin B12 deficiency, unlike people who eat any meat, egg or dairy?
questions.question: Why are strict vegetarians at particular risk of vitamin B12 deficiency, unlike people who eat any meat, egg or dairy?

options.A: Vitamin B12 is made only by microorganisms and reaches the human diet almost exclusively through animal-derived foods, so a diet with no animal products at all provides essentially none
options.B: Plant foods actively destroy any vitamin B12 present in a meal
options.C: Vegetarians absorb B12 normally but excrete it far faster than meat-eaters
options.D: Vitamin B12 requirements are higher in vegetarians than in meat-eaters

explanations.A: Correct. Vitamin B12 is synthesised only by certain bacteria and archaea, never by plants, so in practice it enters the human food supply through animal products (meat, eggs, dairy) whose own B12 ultimately derives from bacterial synthesis in the animal's gut or diet. A diet that excludes all animal products therefore provides essentially no dietary B12, and because the body's B12 stores (mainly in the liver) are large enough to last several years, deficiency in a strict vegetarian typically develops slowly, over years, rather than suddenly.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Plant foods do not destroy B12; the issue is that they simply never contained any to begin with, since plants cannot synthesise it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. There is no evidence that a vegetarian diet increases B12 excretion; the deficiency arises from inadequate intake, not increased loss.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vitamin B12 requirements do not differ between vegetarians and meat-eaters; the difference is entirely on the supply side, in what the diet provides.

questions.learning_objective: Explain why a strict vegetarian diet, containing no animal products, provides essentially no dietary vitamin B12.
questions.source_citation: EOM - Blood End Egyptian 1, Q10 (Alexandria University, AU-MED-103).

questions.title: The pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is classified as which type of reaction, and which listed cofactor is NOT one it actually requires?
questions.question: The pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is classified as which type of reaction, and which listed cofactor is NOT one it actually requires?

options.A: Oxidative decarboxylation; biotin is not one of its five required cofactors
options.B: Simple decarboxylation with no oxidation; thiamine pyrophosphate is not required
options.C: Oxidative decarboxylation; NAD+ is not one of its five required cofactors
options.D: Reductive carboxylation; biotin is not required

explanations.A: Correct. The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex performs an oxidative decarboxylation: pyruvate loses a carboxyl group as CO2 while its remaining two carbons are oxidised and transferred onto coenzyme A to form acetyl-CoA. This one irreversible reaction genuinely requires five cofactors -- thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, coenzyme A, FAD and NAD+ -- but biotin, despite being a classic decarboxylation-reaction cofactor elsewhere in metabolism (it is pyruvate carboxylase's cofactor, a different enzyme entirely), is not one of them; offering biotin as a distractor tests exactly this commonly confused pair.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The reaction is an oxidative decarboxylation, not decarboxylation alone, since pyruvate is genuinely oxidised in the process; and thiamine pyrophosphate is very much required, being the coenzyme most sensitive to deficiency in this reaction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. NAD+ is one of the five genuine cofactors this reaction requires, so it is the wrong answer to 'which is NOT required'; biotin, not NAD+, is the cofactor that does not belong to this list.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The reaction removes a carboxyl group (decarboxylation) and oxidises the remainder; it is not a carboxylation reaction of any kind, reductive or otherwise.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the PDH reaction as an oxidative decarboxylation and identify biotin, not one of its five true cofactors, as the classic confusable distractor (it is pyruvate carboxylase's cofactor instead).

questions.title: Two citric acid cycle reactions release CO2 as an oxidative decarboxylation. Which two enzymes catalyse them?
questions.question: Two citric acid cycle reactions release CO2 as an oxidative decarboxylation. Which two enzymes catalyse them?

explanations.A: Correct. Isocitrate dehydrogenase converts isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate, releasing the cycle's first CO2 and generating NADH; alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase then converts alpha-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA, releasing the cycle's second CO2 and generating a second NADH. These are the only two CO2-releasing steps in the entire cycle, both of which are oxidative decarboxylations chemically resembling the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction, and both are irreversible, tightly regulated control points.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Citrate synthase condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate without releasing CO2, and succinate dehydrogenase oxidises succinate to fumarate without releasing CO2; neither is a decarboxylation step.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fumarase hydrates fumarate to malate, and malate dehydrogenase oxidises malate to oxaloacetate; neither releases CO2.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aconitase isomerises citrate to isocitrate without releasing CO2, and succinate thiokinase's substrate-level phosphorylation step also releases no CO2.

questions.learning_objective: Name isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase as the citric acid cycle's two CO2-releasing (oxidative decarboxylation) steps.

questions.title: Which enzyme performs the first, and rate-limiting, step of haemoglobin catabolism, and what does it produce?
questions.question: Which enzyme performs the first, and rate-limiting, step of haemoglobin catabolism, and what does it produce?

options.A: Heme oxygenase, acting in the reticuloendothelial system, producing biliverdin, carbon monoxide and free iron
options.B: Glucuronyl transferase, acting in the liver, producing conjugated bilirubin
options.C: Bilirubin reductase, acting in the intestine, producing urobilinogen
options.D: Ferrochelatase, acting in the bone marrow, producing haem

explanations.A: Correct. When senescent red cells are broken down in the reticuloendothelial system (spleen, liver and bone marrow macrophages), heme oxygenase catalyses the first and rate-limiting step of haem catabolism, opening the porphyrin ring to release biliverdin, carbon monoxide (the only significant endogenous source of CO in the body) and free iron, which is recycled back into the iron pool. Biliverdin is then rapidly reduced to bilirubin, which travels on to the liver for the next stage of the pathway.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glucuronyl transferase acts later, in the liver, conjugating bilirubin with glucuronic acid to make it water-soluble for excretion; it is not the first step and does not act in the reticuloendothelial system.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bilirubin reduction to urobilinogen by gut bacteria happens last, in the intestine, well downstream of haem catabolism's first step.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ferrochelatase inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX during haem synthesis, the opposite pathway; it plays no role in breaking haem back down.

questions.learning_objective: Name heme oxygenase as the first, rate-limiting enzyme of haem catabolism and state its three products (biliverdin, CO, iron).

questions.title: The red cell's glutathione system depends on a steady supply of NADPH. Where does this NADPH come from, and what does reduced glutathione then do?
questions.question: The red cell's glutathione system depends on a steady supply of NADPH. Where does this NADPH come from, and what does reduced glutathione then do?

options.A: NADPH from the hexose monophosphate shunt's oxidative phase; reduced glutathione neutralises peroxides and other oxidants that would otherwise damage haemoglobin and the cell membrane
options.B: NADPH from glycolysis's substrate-level phosphorylation steps; reduced glutathione generates ATP directly
options.C: NADPH from the citric acid cycle; reduced glutathione regenerates 2,3-BPG
options.D: NADH, not NADPH, from anaerobic glycolysis; reduced glutathione binds oxygen in place of haemoglobin

explanations.A: Correct. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, the hexose monophosphate shunt's first and rate-limiting oxidative-phase enzyme, is the red cell's main source of NADPH. Glutathione reductase then uses that NADPH to keep the cell's glutathione pool in its reduced (GSH) form, and reduced glutathione is what neutralises hydrogen peroxide and other oxidants (via glutathione peroxidase) before they can oxidise hameoglobin's iron or damage the red cell membrane -- which is exactly the protection that fails when G6PD deficiency limits NADPH supply, leading to oxidant-induced haemolysis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glycolysis's substrate-level phosphorylation steps produce ATP, not NADPH (they use ADP as the phosphate acceptor, not NADP+); and reduced glutathione's role is antioxidant defence, not ATP generation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The citric acid cycle is not relevant to the mature red cell, which has no mitochondria; the red cell's NADPH comes specifically from the hexose monophosphate shunt.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is specifically NADPH, not NADH, that the glutathione system depends on, and glutathione does not bind oxygen -- that remains haemoglobin's role.

questions.learning_objective: Trace NADPH from the HMP shunt's oxidative phase through glutathione reductase to reduced glutathione's antioxidant role, protecting haemoglobin and the membrane.
